Average maturity is not a payment calendar: the same mean can hide a cash gap

Compare two original principal schedules with identical face totals and mean maturities, then inspect their receipt dates, cash paths and deadline funding needs in four interactive charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two principal calendars with the same face-weighted mean maturity

Two original principal-only receipt schedules, already assumed held at time zero. One splits the entered future principal equally between mean year minus spacing and mean year plus spacing. The other receives all principal at the mean year. Face amounts, rather than purchase prices or market values, determine the stated weighting. Purchase costs and pricing are absent, so equal face totals and mean dates do not imply equal investment costs or returns. All principal is assumed paid in full and on time. A single bill is due in the entered whole year; receipts in that same year arrive immediately before the bill. Opening cash and earlier receipts remain available without interest. The fixed twelve-year chart includes every permitted receipt and bill. Negative cash records an unfunded payment requirement; the model supplies no loan, early sale, overdraft or delayed payment. No coupons, reinvestment, taxes, inflation, default, calls, settlement delays, fund redemptions or bond-price sensitivity is modeled. The mean is not modified duration or proof of cash-flow matching.

The central idea

A weighted average condenses dates into one number. Funding a particular bill requires enough cash by its actual deadline, even when a later receipt makes the final balance look adequate.

01

Ask which dates disappeared inside the average

An average maturity can be a useful summary of a set of future principal payments. It does not identify every date when money arrives. Two schedules can share the same average while providing different amounts at a particular spending deadline.

This article constructs that difference directly. Each calendar contains CAD 20,000 of promised future principal. One receives CAD 10,000 in year four and CAD 10,000 in year eight. The other receives the full CAD 20,000 in year six.

Weighting by face amounts gives the first calendar a mean maturity of 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 8 = six years. The single-receipt calendar also has a six-year mean. Neither that equality nor the equal face total establishes that the investments would have identical purchase prices.

The calendars are assumed already held at time zero. No purchase is funded inside this illustration. The model therefore compares receipt timing and payment needs, without ranking investment returns or acquisition costs.

02

State what is included before using principal as a resource

Investor.gov’s bond overview describes principal promised at maturity and also discusses the risk of missed payments. This example assumes every stated principal amount is paid in full on its chosen date. It does not assess an actual issuer.

The schedule contains principal receipts only, with no coupons or other income. This is a deliberately narrow calendar rather than a complete model of any coupon-bearing portfolio. Face amount is the future payment quantity, not necessarily the cash originally invested.

Earlier receipts remain in cash without interest. Later claims are not sold early, pledged for a loan or treated as available cash before their dates. Reinvestment returns, tax, call provisions and settlement delays are excluded.

The receipt bars make the distinction visible. In year six, the first calendar has received only half its face total. Its remaining CAD 10,000 is still scheduled for year eight, even though its average maturity is year six.

03

Place the bill after the cash that is actually available

The separate opening cash reserve is CAD 2,000. A single CAD 20,000 payment is due in year six. Within a year, any scheduled principal receipt is assumed to arrive immediately before that bill.

The two-tranche calendar has received CAD 10,000 by the deadline. Combined with the opening CAD 2,000, it has CAD 12,000 available. After allowing for the CAD 20,000 bill, its position is −CAD 8,000.

The single-receipt calendar receives CAD 20,000 in year six before the bill. Its cash becomes CAD 22,000 and then falls to CAD 2,000 after payment. It needs no additional opening cash under that order of events.

The two means remain six years throughout this comparison. The difference comes from how much of each schedule has matured by the deadline. An average date cannot release the second tranche two years early.

04

An equal final balance does not remove a past funding problem

The cash chart extends to year twelve so every permitted principal receipt and bill lies inside its window. After the year-eight principal arrives, the two-tranche ledger returns from negative CAD 8,000 to positive CAD 2,000.

Both schedules finish with the same arithmetic endpoint: opening CAD 2,000 plus CAD 20,000 principal less the CAD 20,000 bill equals CAD 2,000. That equality is a useful conservation check.

It does not mean the first bill was actually financed. A negative segment records the cash that was missing when payment was due. The model does not supply a loan, arrange an overdraft, delay the bill or ignore the temporary gap.

Providing an additional CAD 8,000 at the start would make the two-tranche calendar fund this specific payment under the selected assumptions. That extra resource needs its own source and cannot also be allocated to another goal without reconciliation.

05

Vary the spread around the mean rather than changing the mean itself

The spacing control moves the two equal tranches symmetrically around the selected mean year. At mean six and spacing one, the principal dates are years five and seven. At spacing three, they are years three and nine.

In both cases, the face-weighted mean stays six. With the default bill in year six, half the principal has arrived by the deadline and half has not. Their cash-funding result is therefore the same in this limited example, despite different distances from the deadline.

The single-receipt calendar does not always need less cash. Move the bill to year five: the two-tranche calendar needs an extra CAD 8,000, while the year-six-only receipt needs CAD 18,000 because none of its principal has arrived. The deadline determines the comparison.

Zero spacing places both halves in year six. They combine into the same payment date as the single-receipt calendar, and the two ledgers coincide. The data table merges equal years instead of presenting the two halves as separate extra money.

The matrix changes the bill year and spacing while keeping the common mean selected. A bill after both tranches arrive may need no additional cash. A bill before either receipt can need substantially more. No cell is a probability, investment loss or measure of portfolio duration.

06

Keep the weighting rule separate from interest-rate sensitivity

The mean in this example weights dates by the face principal promised at each date. Because the two tranches have equal face amounts, each receives weight one-half. Another reporting convention could use different weights, so record the definition beside an average.

The CFA Institute’s public interest-rate-risk overview defines Macaulay duration using present-value weights on bond cash flows. This principal calendar instead uses face amounts and contains neither market prices nor yields. It calculates neither Macaulay nor modified duration. Matching its mean to a deadline does not establish a duration-matching or immunization strategy.

The model also does not estimate what an early sale might raise. Selling an outstanding claim before maturity would require a market value, dealing costs and an actual settlement date. Those new facts could change the cash available and add risks beyond the promised principal calendar.

A plan can therefore need separate reviews of payment timing, market-price exposure and issuer risk. One average number does not settle all three questions.

07

Use exact usable-cash dates before committing to a payment

The whole-year labels keep the explanation simple. Real bills and maturities have dates within the year. A December maturity cannot fund a March payment merely because both labels carry the same calendar year.

Confirm when proceeds become usable, what currency they arrive in and whether tax or costs reduce the amount available. Keep money needed earlier accessible unless a separate, confirmed funding arrangement covers the gap.

The amount of the bill and the opening cash are independently entered. The illustration does not establish affordability, verify an actual security, compare purchase costs or recommend a ladder versus a single holding.

Use the receipt table, the cash path and the deadline bridge together. A summary maturity can help describe the holdings, while the dated ledger shows whether those holdings supply the particular payment when it is needed.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical figures compare principal-only promises without purchase pricing, coupon income or early sales. The stated average is weighted by future face amounts and is not a duration calculation or an available investment recommendation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
